Chapter One: Growing Up in a World Shaped by Slavery and Survival
When you picture childhood, you probably think of carefree days filled with play and discovery. But imagine what it was like for a child born into slavery—where every day meant keeping your head down, boundaries everywhere, and a constant need to stay alert. On the marshy shores of Maryland in the early 1800s, a little girl named Araminta—who the world would come to know as Harriet Tubman—took her first steps into this world. For her, freedom wasn’t just out of reach; it was barely even a rumor. Each day was about making it through, one moment at a time.
The details of Harriet’s earliest years are a bit blurry, but one thing’s for sure—the emotions run deep. Imagine growing up in a place where your greatest comfort is your family, but you live with the fear of losing them at any moment. Enslaved families crowded together in small cabins, where nighttime brought whispered stories—of ancestors, warnings about overseers, and the tiniest flicker of hope for escape. If you were a child, your whole world was shaped by the demands of people who claimed you as property. Even a mother’s hug could be cut short by the call of the master or the cry of a sibling in pain. Adults moved with a quiet caution, always watching, always listening, never safe.
Picture this: a little girl, barely big enough to carry a bucket, is sent to fetch water. The path is slippery and muddy. The bucket feels impossibly heavy. She knows if she spills even a drop, punishment could be waiting. When the water sloshes out—because how could it not?—her heart pounds. Even these tiny mistakes could have big consequences. But this is how resilience starts to grow, not because she chooses it, but because she has to.
Family meant everything, even though it could break your heart. Parents did what they could to protect their children from the harshest realities, but the threat of being sold away hung over every moment. Sometimes, a brother or sister would just vanish—sent to another plantation. The family would grieve quietly, afraid to show too much emotion. These losses left invisible scars, but they also sparked a fierce determination to hold on tight to the ones who remained.
Slavery’s cruelty wasn’t just about the body—it was about the mind, too. Kids learned to read a room fast: the look in an overseer’s eyes, the way an adult tensed up, the sudden hush in a conversation. They found tiny ways to push back. Maybe it was sneaking a quick break, sharing a secret with a friend, or just letting themselves imagine a different life. For Araminta, these moments became lessons in power, injustice, and the true meaning of freedom.
As she got older, the work just got tougher. Jobs that once seemed impossible became the new normal, and childhood faded away before it even really began. The outside world was mostly a mystery, but every now and then, stories of escape and resistance would drift in—shared by travelers or whispered by the elders. Those stories became lifelines, proof that things could change.
The truth is, not much is left of Harriet’s early life in the history books. The records are thin, and the memories that do survive are often patchy. But what does shine through is her unbreakable spirit. Even as a young girl, Harriet refused to accept the world as it was. Against all odds, she learned to survive, to care for others, and to imagine a future where freedom wasn’t just a dream—it was something worth fighting for.
